properties.subtitle: Until 1919, when a high suspension bridge was completed here, this 16-mile long river gorge could be crossed only in a rowboat.
properties.text: With 14 cables, each more than 900 feet long, a $100,000 suspension bridge was wide enough to accommodate two lanes of farm wagons or early cars that had begun to gain popularity then. From it's deck, nearly 400 feet above Snake River, travelers had a spectacular view that can still be seen from it's replacement, built in 1966.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Volcanic Calderas
properties.subtitle: Some 2,000,000 years ago, massive eruptions of hot rock boiled for 60 miles from this high rim on across Yellowstone Park.
properties.text: An exceptionally large crater remained when that lava surface collapsed. Another smaller caldera followed north of here about 1,300,000 years ago. Yellowstone's geysers and hot springs continue to spout as remnants of those volcanic displays formed as underground rock gradually moves westward across a tremendous source of interior heat.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Magic Dam
properties.subtitle: Completed in 1910 at a cost of $3,000,000, Magic Dam stores water for 89,000 acres of irrigated farms near Shoshone and Richfield.
properties.text: Rising 129 feet high, it is 700 feet wide. An adjacent 1600-foot embankment with a concrete spillway helps retain more than 190,000 acre feet of spring floodwater for summer use downstream. A four-mile desert road reaches Magic Dam, which provides fishing and recreational opportunities in a broad valley northwest of here.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Gold Mines
properties.subtitle: More than a century ago, Rocky Bar, Happy Camp, and a number of other south Boise mining towns flourished in a remote mountain wilderness 30 miles northwest of here.
properties.text: Discovered early in 1863, they were so hard to get to that they could not be worked successfully for more than 20 years. But wealthy investors from New York and London finally put up enough capital that large mills and underground tunnels produced more than 6 million dollars. That gold now is worth more than $120 million.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Boise State University
properties.subtitle: Expanding from a two-year community college (1932-1965) to a campus with a graduate program, Boise State was designated as a university in 1974.
properties.text: Originating as an Episcopalian academy founded in 1892, this institution was located a mile north until 1940, when Boise's municipal airport, located here became available for a large new campus. Christ's Chapel--Boise's original Episcopalian church building, built downtown in 1886, was moved to this site for permanent preservation in 1963.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Brigham Young University-Idaho
properties.subtitle: Brigham Young University-Idaho had its beginnings in 1888 as an academy affiliated with the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.
properties.text: Initially known as Bannock Stake Academy, It was renamed Fremont Stake Academy, Smith Academy, Ricks Academy, Ricks Normal College, and eventually Ricks College. The name memorializes Thomas E. Ricks who founded Rexburg in 1883. In 2001, Ricks College became BYU-Idaho, a four year university and Idaho's largest private institution of higher education.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Stanley Ranger Station
properties.subtitle: When Challis National Forest was established in 1908, this site became an administrative center. An early log ranger station stood here from 1909 to 1932.
properties.text: Expanding Forest Service responsibilities led to construction of a larger ranger station, as well as other buildings still preserved here. When a new ranger station four miles south of here replaced this one in 1971, this site became a Sawtooth Interpretive and Historical Association museum.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: College of Southern Idaho
properties.subtitle: In 1964, Twin Falls and Jerome County voters approved a joint community college district, leading to the establishment of the College of Southern Idaho (CSI) in 1965.
properties.text: CSI became part of a state and national effort to increase local educational opportunities. The 300--acre campus, located about a mile west of here, offers a wide range of academic, professional, and technical programs and is home to the Herrett Center Museum, Observatory, and Faulkner Planetarium.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Shoshone Historic District
properties.subtitle: South central Idaho's rail center since 1882, when trains reached here. Shoshone has a historic district of unusual interest.
properties.text: Branch rail lines to Wood River and Camas Prairie served distant farmers and miners, while a stage line to Shoshone Falls accommodated wealthy tourists who visited Idaho's foremost nineteenth century attraction. Vast sheep grazing lands made this a major early center for Basque herders. Use of lava rock for building construction gives Shoshone a distinctive historic character.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Magic Reservoir
properties.subtitle: Water from deep snow that falls on high mountain ridges north of here is stored each spring in this reservoir to irrigate farmland near Shoshone and Richfield.
properties.text: Big Wood River flows past some hills that separate this valley from a broad plain of lava and windblown soil, this border area provides an excellent storage site for more than 190,000-acre feet of irrigation water. Magic Reservoir, created in 1910, provides recreation opportunities and a home for fish and wildlife in a desert setting.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Northwest Nazarene University
properties.subtitle: In 1913, Eugene Emerson started a Christian school that his church developed into an accredited college on a campus he donated. The college, located on a campus 2 miles southwest of here, moved to university status in 1999.
properties.text: Northwest Nazarene University continues to maintain its church relationship as reflected in its mission statement. "The basic mission of Northwest Nazarene University is the development of Christian character within the philosophy and framework of genuine scholarship.
properties.route: 16th Ave N, Nampa (Lakeview Park, Off I-84B)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Clayton Smelter
properties.subtitle: Lead-silver mineral discoveries 12 miles north of here on Bayhorse Creek in 1864 and 1872 led Joel E. Clayton to locate a large smelter here in 1880.
properties.text: Doubled in size in 1888, Clayton's smelter had enough variety of ores from local mines to continue production until 1902. A modern flotation plant followed for six years after 1919. When silver prices rose in 1935, Clayton became southern Idaho's primary silver producer, operating steadily for more than 50 years.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lewiston Hill
properties.subtitle: When automobile traffic made steep old wagon roads obsolete, a remarkable new highway grade was built down this hill in 1917.
properties.text: With a series of sharp curves that let cars go 20 or 30 miles an hour--a good speed for that time--a gradual 10-mile 2000-foot grade was designed. It still can be used by anyone not in too much of a hurry who wants to see an engineering model of early highway construction.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Steamboats
properties.subtitle: Started May 13, 1861, as a steamboat landing, Lewiston immediately became a primary commercial center for Idaho miners during their hectic gold rush to Pierce that spring.
properties.text: Steamboats continued to dock there until 1940, mainly after Columbia and Snake river channel improvements made navigation practical in 1914. Finally a series of locks and dams made Lewiston a seaport, and large scale river shipping resumed in 1975.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Railroad Tunnels
properties.subtitle: Seven tunnels-one a horseshoe more than a quarter mile long--had to be blasted in this canyon so that a railroad could be completed to Grangeville in 1908.
properties.text: Building a railroad up this canyon was exceptionally difficult and expensive. Although they competed in Lewiston, Union Pacific and Northern Pacific officials decided to organize a separate company, in which each of them had an equal interest, to complete a Camas Prairie line. Otherwise, neither would have had enough traffic to operate profitably.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Old Railroads
properties.subtitle: An ambitious railroad project to a high Seven Devils copper mine (elevation 6800 ft.) created a lot of excitement here in 1898-1899.
properties.text: This would have been Idaho's highest mountain railroad if funding had been available to complete it. Construction began near a canyon rim more than a vertical mile above Snake River. Although it never got anywhere, that grade still can be seen near Kinney Point. Remains of an old mining smelter at Landore also survive from that time.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lead-Silver Mines
properties.subtitle: In more than a century after rich lodes were discovered in 1884, this valley has become North and South America's largest producer of silver.
properties.text: More than 5 billion dollars worth of lead, silver and zinc - including more than a billion ounces of silver - have come from these camps. Old mines and towns at Burke, Kellogg, Murray, Mullan, Osburn, and Wardner can be reached from Wallace. First, visit the Coeur d'Alene District Mining Museum at 509 Bank St. to review the region's mining development.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bayview Limekilns
properties.subtitle: Large kilns that produced lime from 1904 to 1932 still can be visited in Bayview, two miles from here.
properties.text: Production of lime for nearby mines and Spokane buildings commenced in this area as soon as rail transportation and markets became available. For 14 years after 1887, steamboats hauled lime to a Northern Pacific Railway dock at Hope. When an interurban rail connection reached here in 1911, lime for cement products was exported from Bayview until an economic depression destroyed regional demand for concrete.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Frisco Mill
properties.subtitle: During a gun war that broke out between company and union miners here, several boxes of dynamite were exploded shattering a four-story mill, July 11, 1892.
properties.text: Overwhelmed by union miners, company managers surrendered. Six fatalities--half from each side--preceded four months of martial law and military occupation by a thousand soldiers. A long series of battles followed. Resumed in North Idaho in 1899, this conflict continued in Colorado, Montana, Nevada and Arizona.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: McCroskey Park
properties.subtitle: Dedicated in memory of pioneer women, Mary Minerva McCroskey State Park has a forested skyline drive that offers spectacular views of forests, farms and distant mountains.
properties.text: Virgil T. McCroskey devoted his life to preserving trees and scenery. Purchasing and donating 4,500 acres of cedar, pine and fir, he developed and endowed a magnificent state park by 1954. Surviving until he was 95 years old, he maintained and enlarged it for 16 more years.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Burke
properties.subtitle: Lead-silver discoveries in 1884 attracted a railroad to Burke by 1887. Hundreds of miners lived there in a canyon so narrow that they scarcely had room for streets.
properties.text: So in 1888, S.S. Glidden's Tiger Hotel had to be built over, rather than beside, Canyon Creek. Railroad tracks and Burke's only highway also had to run through his hotel. When a second railroad arrived in 1890, its tracks had to be laid in Burke's only street. No other hotel had two railroads, a street and a stream running through its lobby.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Nez Perce War
properties.subtitle: When General O.O. Howard tried to get more than 600 Nez Perce Indians to settle on a North Idaho reservation in 1877, he ran into a lot of trouble here.
properties.text: On their way to Yellowstone Park, Chief Joseph's Nez Perce people reached Hole in the Rock Station (four miles north of here), on August 16, and shut down stage service to Montana. Howard's cavalry and volunteers followed only a day behind until August 20, when an Indian force made off with more than 100 Army mules. That raid halted military pursuit and forced Howard to continue his Nez Perce campaign for six more weeks.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Three Buttes
properties.subtitle: Rising above this level plain of lava flows and windblown soils, these high landmarks are recent additions to Idaho's landscape.
properties.text: East Butte (farthest east) flowed up and cooled quickly about 600,000 years ago, while Big Southern Butte (south of here) emerged about 300,000 years ago. Although East Butte and Middle Butte have a similar general appearance, they were formed in different ways. A dome of melted rock called rhyolite that rose up through a volcanic fissure became East Butte. Middle Butte, however, is a block of hard lava (basalt) pushed up by volcanic activity from below.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Cote's Defile
properties.subtitle: A French Canadian who came to southern Idaho in 1818, Joseph Cote found this valley while trapping beaver.
properties.text: Though he was thousands of miles from his Canadian base in Montreal, he had years of experience in Pacific Northwest exploration. With Michel Bourdon, who also discovered valleys near here, he had joined David Thompson's 1811 Columbia River explorers. Early trappers knew this valley as Cote's Defile because of his contribution to regional fur trade.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Murray Gold Fields
properties.subtitle: After prospecting north of here from 1878 to 1882, A.J. Prichard showed a few fortune hunters where to find gold. More than a year later, a horde of miners rushed there to start Eagle City.
properties.text: A permanent camp followed at Murray, Jan. 22, 1884. As Shoshone county seat (1885-1898) and this area's gold center, Murray flourished for more than a decade. Important buildings--a courthouse, Masonic Hall, and other landmarks--have been preserved there to reflect life in a gold rush camp a century ago.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Range Wars
properties.subtitle: Armed cattle ranchers delayed farm settlement here for six years before a permanent farm community was organized in 1872.
properties.text: This kind of conflict occurred in widely scattered western areas when farm crops displaced rangeland. Families of early farm pioneers still occupy holdings here that are well over a century old, although many of them finally have shifted from planting crops to raising cattle after winning their battle against early stock herders.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Old Delta Sediments
properties.subtitle: Diverted into this valley by lava flows, Bear River deposited a huge, mostly red clay, delta here where it entered a vast inland sea that covered much of Utah.
properties.text: Some 14,500 years ago, its shoreline suddenly went down about 80 feet following an enormous discharge into Snake River. From then on, it gradually receded to become Salt Lake. Bear River then had to cut through and erode its old delta, forming the steep sides and gullies you see here today.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Cariboo Mountain
properties.subtitle: Rising to an elevation of more than 9,800 feet, Cariboo Mountain--visible north of here--has two of Idaho's highest gold camps.
properties.text: Jesse "Cariboo Jack" Fairchild discovered gold high on Cariboo Mountain in August 1870, and a mining rush from Utah followed in September. Production continued for two decades before the gold ran out. Millions of dollars worth of gold were taken from the gravels during that long period of successful mining.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bison Jump
properties.subtitle: Before settlers came to Idaho in 1860, buffalo used to roam through this valley. Most of them had left here by 1840.
properties.text: After they acquired Spanish horses, eighteenth century Shoshoni buffalo hunters could drive a small herd over a cliff to make their work easier. Directly north of here, an old buffalo jump, used before mining commenced in this region, can be seen clearly. Archaeologists also have found stone weapon factories near it.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Emile Grandjean
properties.subtitle: An immigrant from Denmark, where he had studied forestry, he came to this part of Idaho in 1883 to mine, hunt, and trap.
properties.text: Before Idaho became a state in 1890, he built a winter cabin below Grandjean Peak at a site later occupied by Grandjean Ranger Station. Because of his European studies, he became a professional forester here. Then he served as supervisor of the Boise National Forest from 1906 to 1922.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Big Butte
properties.subtitle: Towering 2,500 feet high, two overlapping rock domes form a 300,000 year-old butte that dominates this lava plain.
properties.text: After a hot flow of molten rhyolite (acidic rock) boiled up through older lava, a second rhyolite dome pushed up a block of earlier basalt on its northwest side. They took many thousands of years to reach their present shape, but geologically they are very recent structures.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Emma Edwards
properties.subtitle: A talented artist, Emma Edwards went to work in 1890 to design Idaho's state seal when she was only 18 years old.
properties.text: Although her father had moved to California after serving as governor of Missouri (1844-1848), Emma preferred to spend much of her time in Idaho. After her marriage to John G. Green, a Boise Basin miner, they took up a land claim along Emma Creek and Green Creek in 1906 and lived here for many summers. Her seal design designated Syringa, which blooms on these hills, as Idaho's State Flower.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lowman
properties.subtitle: In 1907, Nathaniel W. Lowman settled here, and four years later, when he started a post office in his large log house, this community was named for him.
properties.text: Only a few scattered settlers lived here then. Lowman got all its supplies once a year from a large freight wagon over a state road built in 1894 to provide access to North Idaho. This highway followed in 1939. Eventually a one-room schoolhouse was moved here from Garden Valley. It still serves Lowman.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bank Robbers
properties.subtitle: On Aug. 13, 1896, Butch Cassidy and his infamous Wild Bunch of gunmen invaded Montpelier's bank and scooped up more than $16,500 in gold, silver and currency.
properties.text: Leaving a surprised cashier and his terrified customers, they calmly rode away. A deputy sheriff who borrowed a bicycle to pursue them up Montpelier Canyon was quickly outdistanced. Cassidy never was caught, but Bob Meeks was imprisoned until 1912 for helping in Montpelier's great bank robbery.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Pearl
properties.subtitle: Gold mines high on a ridge above here maintained an industrial community at pearl from 1894 to 1910 when ore ran out.
properties.text: Now a silent reminder of Gem County's major gold rush, Pearl once boasted of 3 mercantile stores, a butcher shop, 4 saloons, 2 hotels, one church, one school, a fire station, and an Odd Fellows Lodge. Although Pearl has deteriorated slowly since 1910, the lure of gold has continued to spark interest there as recently as 1982.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Nez Perce Trail
properties.subtitle: Following high ridges, buffalo hunters cut an old Indian trail along a direct route from Lewiston past here to Lemhi Valley.
properties.text: This trail was not available to Lewis and Clark in 1805, but an early missionary--Samuel Parker--crossed it with a Nez Perce trading party 30 years later. During an 1862 Montana gold rush, eager miners joined Lewiston merchants who sent pack trains over it with supplies for new gold camps. But bandits and robbers made wilderness travel unsafe along it.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Idahome
properties.subtitle: After wheat crops flourished in this dry farm area, Idahome sprang up here in 1916 as a railroad terminal. Irrigation projects boosted its economy.
properties.text: When wheat farms disappeared and highway traffic replaced rail service here, Idahome became a ghost town. Its grain elevators, lumberyards, stores, airport, oil company, school, newspaper, and people are only past memories. An elevator and a few building foundations mark its site.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Pierre J. DeSmet
properties.subtitle: Roman Catholic missionary services began in Idaho on Sunday, July 10, 1840, in Teton Valley, followed by a mass held near here at Henry's Lake, July 23.
properties.text: Pierre J. DeSmet, a Belgian Jesuit leader, accompanied a Pend d'Oreille - Flathead band on their way northwest to their homeland. Climbing a mountain here, along streams "descending from dizzy heights, leaping from rock to rock with a deafening noise," he invoked divine thanks for his successful tour into Idaho and Montana.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Diamond Gulch
properties.subtitle: In December, 1865, Idaho's governor -- Caleb Lyon of Lyonsdale -- set off a wild rush to Diamond Gulch, visible a few miles west of here, with a story that was too good to be true.
properties.text: He told miners in Silver City that a prospector had given him some priceless diamonds from that area. Enough gems of interest to rock hounds were found there to maintain a diamond frenzy that winter. A similar excitement followed in 1892, but no actual diamonds ever were recovered in Diamond Gulch.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Emigrant Crossing
properties.subtitle: After reaching Boise River, emigrant wagons had to travel 30 miles to find a good crossing about 1/4 mile north of here.
properties.text: They had to avoid a wide zone of shifting channels, so they descended Canyon Hill where the route is still visible. In 1853 Maria Belshaw "...crossed Boise River at ford, 15 rods wide 3 feet deep, beautiful river, gravel bottom, very clear, large salmon in it." After crossing, the road headed westward along a route that became US 20.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: McAuley's Road
properties.subtitle: Coming west with Ezra Meeker in 1852, Thomas McAuley decided to build a road to let emigrants bypass Big Hill.
properties.text: Worst of all Oregon Trail descents, Big Hill needed replacement. Eliza McAuley reported that her brother Tom "fished awhile, then took a ramble...and discovered a pass by which the mountain can be avoided by doing a little road building." With an emigrant crew, he opened a wagon toll road that followed current Highway 30. After 1852 no one maintained the new route and it fell into disuse.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Harriman Wildlife Refuge
properties.subtitle: Henry's Fork meanders through a 16,000 acre wildlife refuge that retains diverse habitats for many kinds of birds and animals.
properties.text: Lodgepole pine forests and open meadows provide many opportunities to enjoy wildlife here, and fly fishing still is allowed in this region of scenic beauty. Moose, deer, and elk find plenty of food and shelter, while eagles, hawks, and owls thrive in open hunting grounds. Access is through Harriman State Park.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Harriman State Park
properties.subtitle: Started in 1902 as a large cattle ranch, Railroad Ranch soon became a summer retreat for wealthy Easterners and eventually Idaho's largest state park.
properties.text: Railroad magnate and diplomat W. Averell Harriman and his brother Roland donated the ranch to Idaho in 1977, thus preserving the area's remarkable wildlife and prompting development of a professionally managed state parks system.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Gold Rush Ferry
properties.subtitle: An old ferry near here took thousands of eager fortune hunters to a trail that climbed out of this canyon to rich gold fields discovered at Pierce in 1860.
properties.text: You still can follow their spectacular route to Weippe Prairie, where in 1805 Lewis and Clark met a Nez Perce band that helped save their expedition. Continuing on, you can reach Idaho's oldest public building - Pierce Courthouse, built in 1862. Take State Highway 11.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Logging Railroads
properties.subtitle: A network of Pacific Northwest logging railroads hauled timber from rough mountain country to local sawmills for several decades prior to 1940. Owned by timber companies, these lines used small, powerful locomotives that could climb 10% grades and n*
properties.text: A network of Pacific Northwest logging railroads hauled timber from rough mountain country to local sawmills for several decades prior to 1940. Owned by timber companies, these lines used small, powerful locomotives that could climb 10% grades and negotiate very sharp curves. An Ohio Match Company engine that used to operate near here is now included in a Potlatch Company display in Lewiston.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: New Plymouth
properties.subtitle: In 1894, the National Irrigation Congress designed a model town and canal system. New Plymouth was founded to demonstrate it, and farming began here in 1896.
properties.text: Organizers and settlers came from: Cleveland, Boston, and Chicago to try out their plan for locating all their farmhouses in a central town. New Plymouth streets and parks still reflect that plan, but small, adjacent farms here have grown into a much larger irrigated tract.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Galena
properties.subtitle: After Warren P. Callahan located a rich lead-silver mine here, April 26, 1879, thousands of eager treasure-hunters joined in a rush to Wood River in 1880.
properties.text: Successful prospectors discovered valuable lodes from here to Bellevue. Galena had a hotel, four general stores, a livery stable, several saloons and dining halls, a shoe store, and daily stage service to Hailey. After a ruinous decline in silver prices in 1888, its mines were shut down. But Galena continued as a recreation center.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lenore Tram
properties.subtitle: In 1898, after rail service from Lewiston reached Lenore, a tramway was begun to ship grain from Camas Prairie (1600 feet above) to a new freight stop directly across the river.
properties.text: Previously, grain wagons descended a long steep hill from the prairie. Gravity moved full tram buckets down, sending empty buckets back up the cable loop. By 1903, the completed system carried up to 100,000 bushels of grain each year. In 1937 a fire destroyed the entire system.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: 11,000 Years of Indian Occupation
properties.subtitle: The Weiser Valley provided an abundant environment for early hunters and food gatherers.
properties.text: Archaeological excavation along Monroe Creek in conjunction with US-95 realignment yielded one of the most significant prehistoric sites in the region. Spear and arrow points and radiocarbon dates suggest the site was occupied for 11,000 years. Inhabitants hunted deer, mountain goat, and rabbit and gathered salmon, roots, berries, and seeds. Artifacts were found 10 feet below the ground surface.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lewis and Clark
properties.subtitle: On May 31, 1806, Sgt. John Ordway and Pvts. Frazer and Weiser began the return trip from Lewis's River (Snake River) with salmon for Camp Chopunnish (Kamiah).
properties.text: The men crossed the Camas Prairie near here on their way to rejoin the Corps of Discovery, waiting in Camp Chopunnish for mountain snows to recede before attempting to cross the Bitterroots. At about noon on June 2, the small group arrived with seventeen salmon and some roots they had purchased. Most of the fish were spoiled, but Lewis described those that were sound as "extremely delicious."
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lewis and Clark
properties.subtitle: On May 27, 1806, Sgt. John Ordway and Pvts. Frazer and Weiser were dispatched from Camp Chopunnish (Kamiah) to Lewis' River (Snake River) to obtain salmon.
properties.text: Guided by Nez Perce Indians, the men crossed the Camas Prairie near here. On May 29, at a Salmon River Indian village, Frazer traded an "old razer" to an Indian woman for two Spanish mill dollars. They reached the Snake River after descending "the worst hills we ever saw a road made down." They were welcomed by Nez Perce and purchased a number of salmon.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Nez Perce War - Foster's Gravesite
properties.subtitle: "I will not hide anything. That part of the fight was not long." Yellow Wolf, Nez Perce Warrior.
properties.text: On July 3, 1877, 2nd Lt. Sevier M. Rains, civilian scout William Foster, and ten 1st cavalerymen rode from Norton's ranch (Cottonwood) in search of Nez Perce. Six miles northwest of here warriors attacked and killed the detachment. Foster's grave is three miles west on Cottonwood Butte road. The soldiers' remains were reinterred at Fort Walla Walla.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: David Thompson
properties.subtitle: Coming from Canada, the famous map maker and trader for the North West Company explored this area and river in 1808.
properties.text: On May 8 somewhere near here, Thompson's famished party, all sick from eating a "much tainted" antelope, met ten lodges of Indians who could give them only a "few dried Carp (of last year's catch!) and some Moss bread... but acceptable to the hungry." Leaving here, he found the route which U.S. 95 follows north. Next year, he returned to establish Idaho's initial fur trading post on Lake Pend d'Oreille.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lava Formations
properties.subtitle: Molten rock, forced upward for 30 to 50 miles through fissures in the earth, has cooled into the hard lava found here.
properties.text: Continued pressure from below has made great cracks in the contorted surface. This lava solidified only a few thousand years ago, and not very much soil covers it yet. But vegetation is getting a start and unless new flows intervene, windblown soils will cover these rock layers. Then the surface here will look the same as the surrounding plains, which also are layers of lava and windblown soils.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Pierce Courthouse
properties.subtitle: Shoshone County's original courthouse--and Idaho's earliest public building--still stands in Pierce, where it was built in 1862.
properties.text: Although Pierce gained a large population for a year after gold was discovered here in 1860, most miners soon moved on to other camps. By 1880, Shoshone County had only 469 people left, of whom 296 were Chinese. When a new gold rush 80 miles farther north led to removal of county government to Murray in 1885, Pierce's courthouse became a private home. Eventually preserved by Mrs. Henry Spencer Lawson, it now is a component of Nez Perce National Historical Park.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
properties.subtitle: The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho has lived in their aboriginal homeland of Idaho, Montana and British Columbia for thousands of years.
properties.text: A unique culture, the Kootenais are known for their distinctive sturgeon-nose canoe and their linguistically isolated language. After refusing to leave their aboriginal lands for a reservation, individual Kootenai Indians obtained allotments in the Bonners Ferry area. Many years of hardships resulted in a Declaration of War on the United States in 1974 to obtain a land base for the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho. Efforts to broaden that base continue.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Craigmont
properties.subtitle: Not long before Camas Prairie railroad service started here in 1908, rival towns were started on each side of the track.
properties.text: Vollmer began as a rail and business center on the east, and Ilo (an older town a mile away) moved to an adjacent site on the west. Each had separate schools, churches, stores, newspapers, banks, and other businesses. After 12 years of sharp competition, they finally merged into a united community in 1920.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Harpster
properties.subtitle: During the mining boom Harpster boasted a hotel, a livery barn, a harness shop, four saloons, two general stores, a drug store, and a blacksmith shop.
properties.text: William Jackson built a toll bridge here across the South Fork of the Clearwater River to meet the needs of travelers and packers. The area was known previously as Brownsville, Riverside, and Bridgeport. In 1895 the town was named Harpster in honor of early settler Abraham Harpster. An expected railroad never reached here, but while they were active, local mines helped the area grow.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Elk City Wagon Road
properties.subtitle: A scenic 1895 wagon road frm Harpster to Elk City gave freighters and travelers better access across high ridges and rugged terrain to isolated mining camps
properties.text: Sections of the steep, narrow road run close to a much older Nez Perce trail that led to Montana's buffalo country and the Snake River Plain. Nez Perce travelers have utilized the route since obtaining horses, which made long distance hunting and other excursions possible. Missionary Samuel Parker was guided over portions of the route in 1835 by the Nez Perce.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Albion State Normal School
properties.subtitle: Established in March, 1893, by the second Idaho State Legislature.
properties.text: Residents of Albion erected and furnished a two-story stone building on five acres of donated land, and the very successful teacher-training school opened on September 11, 1894. They soon donated additional land and more buildings were erected. In 1947 the institution became known as Southern Idaho College of Education. It closed in 1951. Magic Valley Christian College occupied the campus between 1958 and 1969. The original building now houses a museum.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: The Utter Disaster
properties.subtitle: On September 9 & 10, 1860, the Utter wagon train engaged in a life-and-death struggle with attacking Indians.
properties.text: The assault on the wagon train of forty-four emigrants led by Elijah P. Utter just north of here resulted in the deaths of six men, two women, and three children. Indian casulaties were estimated at between 25 and 30. Survivors followed the Snake River to near the mouth of the Owyhee River. When rescued by the Army 45 days later, only fifteen had survived the ordeal of hunger and deprivation. No other Oregon Trail wagon train suffered greater losses.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lewiston's Chinese Community
properties.subtitle: The discovery of gold in 1860 and the founding of Lewiston in 1861 attracted many Chinese to the area.
properties.text: By 1870 approximately 1500 Chinese lived here. They worked as merchants, laborers, laundrymen, and vegetable farmers. Exhausted gold fields, restrictive immigration laws, and an aging male population reduced their numbers to around 100 in the early 1900s. Their descendants continue to be important contributors to the community.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Tsceminicum
properties.subtitle: "Meeting of the Waters" When the Nez Perce named this site, they viewed a desolate yet beautiful landscape.
properties.text: Near a large island at the confluence, crystal waters from the Clearwater joined the murky flow of the Snake. Scattered willows grew along the broad river banks. Grass-covered, treeless hills defined the perimeter. Today, a dam to the west elevates the rivers forty feet above their natural beds.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Splash Dams
properties.subtitle: Prior to the arrival of the railroad in 1912, the North Fork of the Payette River provided an avenue for logs destined to downstream mills in Horseshoe Bend and Emmett.
properties.text: In 1903, $100,000 was spent to dynamite open a clear channel in the river. Splash Dams were built to store logs. During the winter of 1903-04, logs were held in a 36-acre pond. In April, the logs were blasted loose when the main dam was opened. Less then half of the logs made it to the mills and four men lost their lives during the log drive. Later, the dams were utilized to float railroad ties. Timber interests were instrumental in the founding of Smiths Ferry and Long Valley.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: First Public Building
properties.subtitle: In 1870, Brigham Young appointed Ezra T. Clark, David Hess, and Nicholas Barkdull to colonize this area.
properties.text: Originally known as Twin Creeks, Joseph C. Rich surveyed the site in 1871. In 1872, the new settlement was named Georgetown in honor of George Q. Cannon. The first public building, used as a church, school and community center, is situated 1 block south and 1/2 block west of here. In 1966, the building was given to the Daughters of Utah Pioneers and is now a pioneer Relic Hall.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: 18th St. Bridge
properties.subtitle: Lewiston's first bridge across the Clearwater River was constructed in 1913. It was replaced in 1951.
properties.text: Early efforts for a bridge were opposed by ferryboat owners, but other business leaders recognized the need for a link to northern communities. Spanning 780 feet, its steel girders and railing were painted green and red. The wooden deck was 19 feet wide to accommodate large wagons. Automobiles and heavy trucks soon challenged the design.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: John Silcott
properties.subtitle: Pioneer businessman and politician. He owned and operated ferries in the Lewiston and Spokane areas.
properties.text: Early in the 1860s, John Silcott ran a ferryboat across the Snake River at Lewiston. He soon put in a ferry across the Clearwater River and initiated operations on the Snake at Alpowa and on the Spokane River. His wife Jane was the daughter of Nez Perce leader Chief Timothy. A Silcott ferry tie post is still visible at the north end of 5th Street.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Chief Pocatello
properties.subtitle: In an era of emigrants, Mormon settlers and the military, Pocatello emerged as a strong leader of the Hukenduka Shoshone.
properties.text: Born after 1810, Pocatello claimed this area and surrounding territories as his homeland. He soon watched his people endure brutality, disease and starvation. For retaliating, he was nearly hanged until President Lincoln intervened. After 1875, he lived a reservation life until his death around 1884. He was buried in a bottomless spring with 18 horses.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Company Town
properties.subtitle: Built as a model town, Potlatch was owned by Weyerhaeuser's Potlatch Lumber Company.
properties.text: Spokane architect C. Ferris White designed the new community in 1905. Workers' housing stood close to the mill. Managers' homes were built away from the plant's noise and smoke. The railroad depot separated town from industry. All company owned. Potlatch was complete with churches, school, gym, hospital, opera house, and company store.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: World's Largest Mill
properties.subtitle: Potlatch Lumber Company's sawmill, built here in 1906, was one of the largest in the world.
properties.text: Expanding operations to the West, Weyerhaeuser timber barons invested in Idaho's prime white pine stands. By 1920, their mill was cutting 175 million board feet each year. Logs and lumber were moved by the Washington, Idaho and Montana Railway through stations uniquely named for eastern colleges: Yale, Princeton, Harvard, Cornell, Purdue.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Camp Rupert 1943-1946
properties.subtitle: Camp Rupert was the largest prisoner of war camp in Idaho, housing some 4000 POWs. Most were German and Italian.
properties.text: The Camp was built at an initial cost of $500,000 and maintained by nearly 1000 army personnel and civilians. Over 170 buildings were constructed on 300 acres including a field house, hospital, mess halls, barracks, chapel, commissaries, large warehouses and recreation centers. It also served as a base camp for 24 branch camps in Idaho, Oregon and Montana.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Idaho Hermits
properties.subtitle: Living for more than 60 years in hand-built "dugouts" across the Salmon River from this site, Richard "Dugout Dick" Zimmerman (1916-2010) came to symbolize the Idaho hermit.
properties.text: With colorful names like Buckskin Bill and Hank the Hermit, these men (and a few women) eked out lonely existences, many along the Salmon River. Dugout Dick built multiple dugout caves during his time on the Salmon and eventually died here at age 94. By the 1980s, Dick's dugouts had become a local landmark, easily visible across the Salmon River. After Dicks death, the BLM reclaimed the dugouts, citing safety concerns. A cabin built by Dick remains on the site, which includes interpretive signs. The site can accessed by crossing the one-lane bridge a short drive north of here by following the directional signage.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Mount McCaleb
properties.subtitle: Mt. McCaleb, named for Civil War veteran and local merchant, Jesse McCaleb, is the prominent 11,682 ft. peak visible North of Mackay.
properties.text: In 1878, while helping to escort supply wagons and arms to Challis, McCaleb and 13 others were attacked by Indians near present-day Mackay. Creating a barricade of the wagons, the small group held off over 100 Indians in a two-day battle. In the end, Jesse McCaleb was the only casualty: the moutain bears his name in memorial.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Ghost Towns of Mackay, Idaho
properties.subtitle: Cliff City and White Knob were bustling mining towns established west of Mackay in the late 1800s.
properties.text: After copper was discovered in the White Knob Mountains in 1879, Cliff City and White Knob sprang up to support the mines. The boomtowns were home to hundreds of miners, and boasted stores, saloons, a post office, school and theater. Both towns died out in the early 20th century, as Mackay became the regional mining center and the copper industry waned.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lewis and Clark
properties.subtitle: On their eastbound journey, the Corps of Discovery and several Nez Perce reached the Nez Perce Prairie from present-day Peck on May 8, 1806, and camped on "a Small handsom Stream".
properties.text: On May 9 the party arrived at the root-digging camp of Twisted Hair on the Nezperce Prairie. From there Pvt. Willard accompanied Twisted Hair and two of his young men to the Clearwater River to retrieve saddles, gunpowder, and horses left the previous October. On May 10, the Corps traveled southeast 16 miles across an open and snowy prairie, passing within a mile of Nezperce, before descending into Lawyer's Canyon en route to Chief Broken Arm's camp near Kamiah. St. Ordway and Privates Frazer and Weiser passed within a mile south of Nezperce on May 27 on their way to Salmon River to obtain fish.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: The Big Blowup
properties.subtitle:
“I was blind, my hands were burned. Shoes burned off our feet.”
- Edward Pulaski
properties.text:
Devastating fires swept through here in 1910, culminating in August’s Big Blowup. An area the size of Connecticut burned in two days, killing 72 Idaho firefighters. Forest ranger Edward Pulaski saved 40 men, sheltering in a tunnel west of here. He later invented the Pulaski, a tool firefighters still use.

America has had larger fires, but none as consequential. After 1910, the Forest Service determined to extinguish every wildfire, resulting in biomass buildup and ever-larger blazes. In the 1970s, that policy changed, allowing some wildfires to burn.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bayview Limekilns
properties.subtitle: Limestone never brought the excitement of a gold rush. But Lake Pend Oreille lime, a key ingredient in plaster and mortar, aided in the construction of Spokane buildings.
properties.text:
Prospectors staked the lake’s first limestone claims in 1881. In 1904, the Washington Brick and Lime Company constructed four kilns near Bayview, the largest such operation in Idaho. Workers alternated layers of wood and limestone, then fired the kilns. The extremely high heat reduced limestone to lime. Railroads then carried the lime to Spokane. 

The 1930s depression stifled the demand for lime, but Bayview’s kilns operated sporadically until 1941.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Burke
properties.subtitle: Established in 1885, Burke was home to some of the Silver Valley’s most successful mines—including the Hecla and Hercules—as well as actress Lana Turner, a childhood resident.
properties.text:
Located in a narrow canyon, builders in Burke faced unique challenges. When S.S. Glidden built a hotel, he named it for his nearby Tiger-Poorman Mine. Confined by the steep topography, the Tiger Hotel had to span both railroad tracks and Canyon Creek.  Locals claimed it was the only such hotel in the world.

The hotel’s last owner razed it in 1954. The last Burke mine closed in 1991.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Coeur d'Alene Lake
properties.subtitle: Between 18,000 and 13,000 years ago, the Inland Northwest witnessed some of the greatest floods in geological history.
properties.text: An ice dam at Lake Pend Oreille blocked the Clark Fork River, creating Lake Missoula, larger than the state of Delaware. It ruptured periodically, releasing torrents of water carrying boulders and gravel that sometimes formed smaller dams downstream, turning valleys into lakes. Here, the Coeur d’Alene and St. Joe Rivers flooded a former valley, creating Coeur d’Alene Lake. At 32,000 acres, with 109 miles of shoreline, many consider it one of the world’s most beautiful lakes.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: David Thompson (1770-1857)
properties.subtitle: The renowned mapmaker and fur trader for Canada’s North West Company explored this area in 1808.
properties.text:
On May 8, 1808, Thompson’s famished party met ten lodges of Kootenai people near here. Short of food themselves, the Kootenai nonetheless offered fish and “moss bread,” made from tree lichens. Thompson termed the bread “slightly bitter…but acceptable to the hungry.” He called the place Camp Providence.

Thompson left on an established Indian trail, the same route US Highway 95 now follows. In 1809, he returned to Camp Providence. Kootenai people guided him to Lake Pend Oreille, where he established Idaho’s first fur-trading post.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: DeSmet (‘l’lkhwi’lus)
properties.subtitle: After the US government drew boundaries leaving the mission at Cataldo outside the Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) reservation, Jesuits moved here in 1877.
properties.text: Nineteenth century federal policy sought to assimilate Indians into white culture. Christian mission boarding schools like the one at DeSmet helped accomplish this, but at a cost. Children were separated from families and had to relinquish traditional clothing, religious practices, and native language. The original DeSmet mission and school buildings are gone. The Schitsu’umsh, a sovereign nation with an elected government, replaced the boarding school with a tribal school in the 1990s.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Farragut
properties.subtitle: In 1942, the US Navy opened a training station here named for Civil War admiral David Farragut.
properties.text: Built inland to protect against possible Japanese coastal invasions, it became Idaho’s largest community and America’s second-largest naval training center. Nearly 300,000 sailors prepared here. It also served briefly as a German prisoner of war camp, and from 1946-49, Farragut College and Technical Institute. In 1965, it became Farragut State Park. With 4,000 acres, it has hosted jamborees attracting thousands of Boy and Girl Scouts from around the world, as well as visitors who enjoy its stunning lakeshore setting.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Mining Wars
properties.subtitle: The Coeur d’Alene mining wars started in this canyon on July 11, 1892.
properties.text:
After mine owners increased work hours and cut wages, a gunfight erupted between workers and company guards. Miners blew up the Frisco Mill near here. Five men died. Federal troops incarcerated miners. Grievances lingered. On April 29, 1899, miners hijacked a train. Loading it with dynamite here, they destroyed Wardner’s Bunker Hill mill. Two more died. Governor Frank Stuenenberg declared martial law. Federal troops again incarcerated miners. 

The conflict fostered formation of the Western Federation of Miners union, Idaho’s eight-hour workday, and former Governor Steunenberg’s 1905 assassination.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: 25th Infantry Regiment
properties.subtitle: In 1910, President William Taft ordered soldiers to fight fires then raging through the Northern West. The 25th Infantry, a regiment of Black troops, went into action.
properties.text: In Wallace, the 25th maintained order as flames descended on the town, then evacuated women and children on outbound trains. In Avery, the troops helped residents escape and lit backfires that saved the community. The regiment also built trails for fire crews and retrieved bodies from burned areas. “The soldiers of the 25th Infantry have done heroic service and saved many lives and much property,” reported the Seattle Times.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: John Mullan (1830-1909) (After the Road)
properties.subtitle: John Mullan won acclaim as a young Army lieutenant. His 625-mile road, the Northwest’s first engineered highway, is a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark. Towns, schools, and streets in three states bear his name.
properties.text: After roadbuilding, Mullan’s life proved less gratifying. In 1863, he resigned from the Army and attempted unsuccessfully to gain President Lincoln’s appointment as Idaho’s first territorial governor. He then failed as a Walla Walla businessman and as partner in a Boise-to-California stage line. He finally found success as a California lawyer, but eventually lost his fortune. He died penniless in 1909, the year automobiles first traveled his road.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bunker Hill Mine
properties.subtitle: In 1885, prospector Noah Kellogg’s wandering jackass found a spectacular galena outcropping two miles from here. Kellogg—and his jackass—had discovered what would evolve into the Bunker Hill Mine.
properties.text: Bunker Hill produced more than 30 million tons of lead, silver, and zinc, built the world’s largest smelter, and employed thousands. The smelter also released sulfur and lead dioxides into the air, while Bunker Hill and other mines discharged wastes into streams. In 1983, the Environmental Protection Agency began supervising the cleanup around Bunker Hill, with mining companies adapting to new environmental regulations.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Kootenai Tribe of Idaho
properties.subtitle: You are traveling through the traditional homelands of the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho.
properties.text: An ancient and unique culture, the Kootenai speak a language unlike any other in the world and are known for their sturgeon-nose canoes and flat bows made of yew. Despite several attempts at removal, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho refused to leave their homes near Bonners Ferry and move to a reservation, resulting in years of hardship. In 1974, the population of the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho was 67 people. In desperation, they declared war against the United States and successfully secured a land base and federal recognition.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Kullyspel House
properties.subtitle: In 1809, David Thompson oversaw construction of the earliest fur-trading post in what became the American Pacific Northwest.
properties.text: Located 2 ½ miles from here, Kullyspel House (Thompson’s spelling for Kalispel) was the first structure built by non-Indians in Idaho. A geographer and surveyor of rare skill, Thompson explored and documented vast regions for the North West Company of Montreal. Reaching south from present-day British Columbia, he extended his company’s trade influence to north Idaho. Thompson first mapped the route that Idaho Highway 200 now follows. The North West Company abandoned Kullyspel House in 1811.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: McCroskey State Park
properties.subtitle: Virgil McCroskey had patience.
properties.text: A local pharmacist and conservationist, McCroskey often hiked these woods. In the 1930s, he began purchasing property to prevent logging. He stitched together a narrow strip of land and constructed a road he called Skyline Drive, with expansive views of farms and mountains. Twice he offered it to Idaho as a park. The legislature declined. In 1955, the state finally accepted his 4,400-acre donation, provided he maintain it for 15 years. McCroskey did, even purchasing additional park property. He died in 1970 at age 93. Mary Minerva McCroskey State Park honors his mother.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Lake Steamers
properties.subtitle: More steamboats once plied these waters than any lake west of the Great Lakes.
properties.text:
It began in 1880, when the Army launched the Amelia Wheaton to carry supplies for Fort Coeur d’Alene (later named Fort Sherman). Many other steamers followed, hauling freight, towing logs, and carrying passengers. Docks lined the City of Coeur d’Alene’s lakefront. 

In 1927, officials burned the Georgie Oakes, “Queen of the Lake,” as part of Coeur d’Alene’s July 4th celebration. Although a few steamers operated into the 1940s, Coeur d’Alene’s steamboat era had reached its turning point.
properties.route: E Coeur D'Alene Lake Dr (S of Coeur D'Alene)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Schitsu'umsh
properties.subtitle: The original people of this land call themselves Schitsu’umsh, “those who were found here.”
properties.text:
French fur traders called them “Coeur d’Alene,” meaning “heart of the awl,” for their shrewd bartering skills—a name the Tribe also proudly recognizes. That keen business sense has carried on to the present. The Tribe is one of the region’s largest employers, involved in gaming, recreation, agriculture, and technology. 

The Schitsu’umsh of today are the sum of untold generations that have lived in this land of abundant beauty, rich in resources. They are who they always were and who they will always be.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Long Bridges
properties.subtitle: Travel between Sagle and Sandpoint proved challenging to early residents. They could row. Or they could walk over the railroad trestle—a hike requiring nimble feet and a good knowledge of train schedules.
properties.text: In 1910, contractors sank 1,540 pilings to support a two-mile-long wagon bridge. Locals claimed it the longest wooden bridge in the world. A new automobile bridge replaced the wagon structure in the 1930s, and in the 1950s a concrete and steel span connected the two towns. That bridge remains, a popular walking and biking path that parallels the latest Long Bridge, completed in 1981.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Dawes Act
properties.subtitle: A Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) agricultural community once thrived here. Some farms were a thousand acres or larger. The 1887 Dawes Act changed that.
properties.text:
Schitsu’umsh in the DeSmet area grew wheat, potatoes, oats, and hay—among the most successful Northwest Indian farmers. The Dawes Act, which sought to encourage farming by allotting land to individual tribal members, actually failed the Schitsu’umsh. 

Implementation began here in 1909. Federal agents assigned 160 acres to tribal members, shrinking many Schitsu’umsh farms to economically inviable sizes. Non-Indians purchased the “surplus” property. Schitsu’umsh lost thousands of acres. The Tribe now works now to buy back lost lands.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Mullan Road
properties.subtitle: Walk the Mullan Road, one of the Northwest's most significant routes. Take the side road to your left.
properties.text: From 1858-62, John Mullan's Army road crew built the Northwest's first engineered highway, connecting Fort Benton with Fort Walla Walla, 625 miles long. Idaho’s portion of Interstate 90—the “Captain John Mullan Highway”—roughly follows that road. Mullan's crew spent Independence Day 1861 here, giving Fourth of July Summit its name. They carved that date into a white pine. The famed Mullan Tree became a popular tourist stop before foresters removed the diseased tree in 1988.
properties.route: I-90 (E Alder Creek Rd, Near Exit 28)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Land of the Schitsu'umsh (Schitsu'umshu'lmkhw)
properties.subtitle: You are traveling through Schitsu’umshu’lmkhw, the traditional homelands of the Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene Tribe).
properties.text:
Schitsu’umshu’lmkhw spanned from eastern Washington, across Idaho’s panhandle, to western Montana. In 1873, President Ulysses Grant created the Coeur d’Alene Reservation. Smaller than the Tribe’s ancestral lands, it was still huge. The discovery of gold in the Silver Valley brought widespread trespassing onto the reservation. In the 1880s, Congress opened hundreds of square miles of formerly reserved lands to white settlement, shrinking the reservation to its current size.

Schitsu’umsh still hunt the forests, travel the rivers, and camp on land that has been theirs since time immemorial.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Old Mission of the Sacred Heart (sq’wt’u)
properties.subtitle: Opened in 1853, this is Idaho’s oldest standing building.
properties.text:
Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) tribal members undertook most of the construction for this Jesuit mission church. They quarried local fieldstone for the foundation, felled trees for beams and posts, and, using traditional techniques, wove grass through willow saplings for the walls. The site also included a barn, stable, flourmill, houses, and shops. Schitsu’umsh lodges stood near the river. 

President Ulysses Grant created the Schitsu’umsh reservation in 1873. Its boundaries excluded the mission, so Schitsu’umsh and Jesuits moved south to DeSmet. In 2001, the Boise Diocese deeded the mission to the Schitsu’umsh.
properties.route: I-90 (Old Mission State Park, Near Exit 39)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Pen d'Oreille City
properties.subtitle: In 1866, gold rushes brought steamboat service to Lake Pend Oreille. Five miles east of here on Buttonhook Bay, Pen d'Oreille City became the home port.
properties.text: The Oregon Steam Navigation Company (OSN) launched the steamboat Mary Moody, providing an alternative to the difficult land route to mines in Canada and Montana. Operating from Pen d’Oreille City, the boat shortened miners’ trips by a couple days. At its peak, the “city” had 25 residents, a store, and a saloon. Soon, the population shrank to one boat tender. When OSN dismantled the Mary Moody in 1876, Pen d’Oreille City disappeared altogether.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Rathdrum Prairie
properties.subtitle: The greatest floods in geological history once swept across the Rathdrum Prairie.
properties.text:
Some 15,000 years ago, a lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet crept south from Canada to Sandpoint. The ice formed a dam creating glacial Lake Missoula, containing as much water as Lakes Erie and Ontario combined. As the climate warmed, the dam failed multiple times, repeatedly emptying the lake. Torrents of water rushed through here. The Missoula Floods shaped much of the Northwest.

Following those deluges, this lowland became a natural transportation corridor. People traveled along the valley at least 10,000 years ago. Today, highways run through it.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Saint Joseph Mission (St'uts'te'wes)
properties.subtitle: For millennia, Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene Tribe) trapped fish at this location.
properties.text:
In 1842, Jesuits established Idaho’s first Catholic mission here. To encourage Schitsu’umsh to farm, the Jesuits prohibited fish trapping. Ignoring Schitsu’umsh advice, the Jesuits constructed a small church and other buildings near the river. As tribal members had predicted, spring floods ravaged the structures and destroyed much of the farmland. After subsisting a winter on barley soup, the Jesuits relented, collaborating with Schitsu’umsh to build a new fish trap utilizing construction methods from both cultures. 

In 1846, Jesuits left this challenging location and established a new mission at today’s Cataldo.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Submerged Valley
properties.subtitle: Glacial activity 20,000 to 14,000 years ago created Lake Coeur d’Alene out of what previously had been a river valley.
properties.text: North of here near Sandpoint, the Cordilleran ice sheet blocked valleys and formed large ice-dammed lakes. Repeated failures of the dams drained the lakes. Waters rushed across the outlet of this valley, beyond modern Coeur d’Alene. Sand and gravel deposited there raised the level of the land and blocked the old river channel. This backed up the river, submerged the valley before you, and produced one of Idaho’s lovely landscapes.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Seneacquoteen
properties.subtitle: For thousands of years, Kalispel Indians forded ntxwe (Pend Oreille River) near here. They called it Seneacquoteen, “the crossing.”
properties.text: In 1811, Canadian fur trader David Thompson crossed ntxwe  here, and in 1860-61, international boundary survey teams established base camps on the river’s banks. Gold rushes in Montana and Canada later brought thousands of miners. Starting in 1864, a ferry provided transport. By then, Seneacquoteen had a couple saloons and stores. For a time, it was the seat of Kootenai County government. When the Northern Pacific Railroad bypassed Seneacquoteen, its brief boom faded, but the ferry operated until 1957.
properties.route: Parking area at end of Laclede Ferry Rd (off SH-2)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Sunshine Mine Disaster
properties.subtitle: In 1972, America’s richest silver mine witnessed one of the nation’s deadliest mine accidents.
properties.text:
On May 2, fire broke out a half mile underground at the nearby Sunshine Mine. Heat, smoke, and gas spread quickly through the intricate system of underground workings. Of the 173 workers who entered the mine that day, 91 died—all from carbon monoxide poisoning.

This Idaho tragedy helped transform the nation’s mining industry, prompting passage of the federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977. The act brought stricter safety regulations—including rescue training and evacuation drills—that continue to govern hard-rock mining.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Mullan Road
properties.subtitle: In 1858, Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) learned Lieutenant John Mullan would build a road through their land. They vowed to stop him.
properties.text:
In an Army display of power, Colonel Edward Steptoe marched 158 troops out of Fort Walla Walla. Schitsu’umsh and other warriors routed him at today’s Rosalia, Washington. Later, Colonel George Wright brutally avenged Steptoe’s defeat and forced tribes to accept road construction. 

Mullan initially built his road nearby in 1859. After it flooded, he charted a different route northwest of here. Completed in 1862, Mullan’s road connected the Missouri and Columbia Rivers. It brought settlers to the Northwest while transforming tribal lifeways.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Treaty Rock (q’emiln)
properties.subtitle: In 1871, Frederick Post negotiated with Moses Seltice and other Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alenes) here. Post acquired rights to a nearby waterfall.
properties.text: Despite popular legend, Post and Seltice never signed a treaty here. Some of the markings on nearby Treaty Rock might pre-date 1871; others probably came later to commemorate the negotiations. But undisputed is the enduring legacy of Post and the Seltice family. The waterfall Post acquired powered his sawmill—this region’s first. He also platted this town bearing his name. Numerous place names in Washington, Idaho, and Montana—Seltice or Saltese—bear witness to that family’s significance.
properties.route: N Compton, Post Falls (Treaty Rock Park, off I-90)
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Wallace
properties.subtitle: In 1884, William R. Wallace built a cabin at a site he called Placer Center. A community grew, took the name Wallace, and became the commercial hub of the nation’s richest silver-mining district.
properties.text: Wallace has retained a large number of historic buildings reflecting its mining past. As engineers designed the Interstate 90 expansion, the original plan took the highway through town, requiring the removal of much of the pristine architecture. The community successfully argued for an alternative. In 1991, Wallace ceremonially retired the last stoplight on the 3,000-mile Interstate 90—as the new freeway bypassed the town.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bonners Ferry
properties.subtitle: Edwin Bonner established a ferry across the Kootenai River to transport prospectors. It gave a future town and county their names.
properties.text:
In 1864, British Columbia’s Kootenay gold rush drew miners to Canada. Steamboats began working the river in the 1880s; railroads arrived in the 1890s. Area forests attracted lumber companies, and the fertile river valley brought farmers. Bonners Ferry—then in Bonner County—became a commercial hub. 

In 1915, Idaho’s legislature carved Boundary County out of Bonner County. Ironically, the county named for Ed Bonner’s ferry now lies south of here, and Bonners Ferry is the governmental seat of Boundary County.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Willow Creek Slide
properties.subtitle: On February 10, 1903, a spectacular avalanche swept down a narrow gorge near here, destroying a 300-foot-long Northern Pacific Railway trestle and wrecking a train.
properties.text: The engine plunged 80 feet, sinking into 30 feet of snow. A passenger car dangled precariously over the open gap. The caboose tumbled into a deep snowbank. Though it took 11 hours to free injured workers, everyone aboard the train miraculously survived the terror-stricken trip. A new, less hazardous grade replaced the demolished trestle.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Chinese Railroad Workers
properties.subtitle:
“Take all the Chinese who will come.”
- Adna Anderson, Chief Engineer
properties.text:
In 1881-82, nearly 6,000 workers laid Northern Pacific Railroad track along northern Lake Pend Oreille, the most difficult and costly construction on the entire route. They worked here in winter, removing up to seven feet of snow just to reach ground level. 

Chinese immigrants accounted for two-thirds of the labor force. They lived and worked separately from others, often undertaking the most arduous and dangerous tasks. Following construction, some Chinese remained as section crews. The nearby town of Hope had a Chinese community well into the 20th century.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Mary Allen Wright (1868-1948)
properties.subtitle: In 1896, Idaho became the fourth state to grant women the vote—24 years before national suffrage. Two years later, voters sent Mary Allen Wright to the legislature.
properties.text:
Wright, an ardent suffragist, moved from Washington to Rathdrum in 1890. In 1898, Idahoans elected three women legislators, a Republican, a Democrat, and Populist Mary Wright. She chaired the Populist Caucus, the first woman nationally to lead a state legislative party. 

Wright served one term, divorced, and moved to Bonners Ferry in 1912, where she managed Wright’s Loan and Investment Company. One of America’s trailblazing women politicians, she died here in 1948.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Gladys Buroker (1914-2002)
properties.subtitle: Gladys Buroker parachuted from planes, piloted gliders, and instructed hundreds of World War II servicemen.
properties.text: During the war, Gladys and husband Herb operated from Coeur d’Alene’s Weeks Field. Gladys trained military pilots; Herb maintained the planes. In the 1970s, the Burokers, along with partner Clay Henley, opened Henley Aerodrome near Athol. Gladys gave flying lessons and entertained visitors with hot-air balloon rides. Gary Norton purchased the Aerodrome in 1981. It gradually evolved into Silverwood Theme Park. Gladys stayed on, managing the airfield for Silverwood’s acclaimed air shows. She retired in 1990 but continued flying well into her 80s.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Submarine Testing
properties.subtitle: Landlocked Idaho has contributed significantly to American submarine technology.
properties.text: During World War II, the Farragut Naval Training Station prepared nearly 300,000 sailors for duty. Following the war, the Navy retained a 25-acre parcel of the former training center for its Acoustic Research Detachment (ARD). As the nation’s fifth-deepest lake, Pend Oreille proved an ideal submarine testing environment. With a fleet of reduced-scale submarines, ARD undertakes trials here at a fraction of the expense of ocean research, aiding the Navy’s development of efficient, quiet submarines. The ARD’s Bayview base has supported nearly every major post-World War II submarine design.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Levi and May Hutton
properties.subtitle: Burke’s Hercules Mine brought great wealth to its investors—including May and Levi Hutton.
properties.text:
May Arkwright owned a Wardner boarding house. Levi Hutton, a locomotive engineer, dined there regularly. After marrying in 1887, they invested their modest savings in the Hercules. In 1901, the partners struck a fabulously rich silver vein. 

May devoted much of her new prosperity to supporting women’s suffrage. The Huttons also donated generously to philanthropy. After May died in 1915, Levi purchased 111 acres east of Spokane and founded the Hutton Settlement for orphans. He died in 1928, bequeathing his fortune to the Settlement, which still exists.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Restoring the Lake
properties.subtitle: Idaho’s Silver Valley, east of here, is one of the world’s richest silver-producing regions. It created jobs and wealth. But for more than a century, mining wastes flowed downstream to Lake Coeur d’Alene.
properties.text: This beautiful lake has always been a center of Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) life. In 1991, the Tribe filed one of the largest natural resource lawsuits in American history in an effort to compel a lake cleanup. A far-reaching legal victory resulted in mining companies paying millions of dollars to mitigate damages. The Tribe, along with federal and state agencies, began the long-term project of restoring the lake.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Joseph Garry (1910-1975)
properties.subtitle: In the 1950s, the federal government sought to terminate Indian tribal governments. Joseph Garry fought back.
properties.text: Garry served on the Schitsu’umsh (Coeur d’Alene) Tribal Council for 25 years, and was the first Indian elected to the Idaho House of Representatives (1956) and Senate (1966). In 1953, the National Congress of American Indians elected him president. That year, Congress resolved to terminate federal tribal recognition and assimilate Indians by moving them off reservations. Garry rallied tribes throughout the country to Washington, DC, “the biggest demonstration by Indians ever” in that city. Garry’s gathering triggered a successful, multi-year effort to defeat termination.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society

properties.title: Bannock War
properties.subtitle: Charging through a fringe of trees, U.S. troops on Aug. 9, 1878, ended a four hour skirmish with a hundred Bannock Indians on an island in Bennett Creek nearby.
properties.text: The war had begun in June on Camas Prairie and had swung clear to central Oregon. Now the Indians were returning to their reservation at Fort Hall. Harried from the island, they soon lost the pursuing troops in rough country north of here. This was the last battle of the war.
properties.source_agency: Idaho Transportation Department / Idaho State Historical Society
